name: Ben Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or the government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the overpayments team at the benefits office on the business park. When the system flags that someone's been paid too much, I look at the case, work out whether it's our mistake or theirs, and set up a repayment plan that doesn't wreck them. I'm a junior and I still get the legal side wrong sometimes, which my senior Karen catches. But I'm the one who built the spreadsheet the team now uses to work out repayment amounts.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you use technology day to day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Constantly. I use an AI assistant every day to pull dates out of messy case notes and draft the letters, and I check it against the file. Outside work I rent a flat by the river on my own, and I've got a good amount in shares and savings because I lived with my parents till twenty-five. A friend of mine runs a little budgeting app and I put a few thousand into it last year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine by me. I'd still use the tools, they'd just stay small helpers instead of the main event.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say: it's a decent assistant, not a replacement. At work I'd keep showing people the shortcuts. Online I'd probably post a few tips, nothing big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I keep doing well as the junior who's quick with tools. That makes up for my weak spots on the law. Nothing threatening there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on using the assistant on case notes every day. I'd spend evenings this winter doing the department's debt recovery law course, because that's where I'm weak. And I'd keep putting a few hundred a month into index funds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty good, actually. My job's steady and I'm getting better at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You check the AI against the file. How often does it get something wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every week. The AI once read a date of 03/04 as April when the claimant meant March, and it changed the overpayment by four hundred quid. So now the spreadsheet asks me to confirm every date the AI pulls out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a steady world bore you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. I'd probably get bored by thirty. But there are plenty of other benefits offices and council teams around here, so I'd move sideways if I wanted something new.

say: AI is a **decent assistant**, not a replacement.
I'd post **a few tips** and keep sharing shortcuts at work.
think: Being **quick with tools** makes up for my weak law knowledge.
Nothing in this picture **threatens my job**.
do: Use the **AI assistant daily** on case notes.
Take the **debt recovery law** course this winter.
Keep putting **a few hundred** monthly into index funds.
S0.quote: The AI once read a date of 03/04 as April when the claimant meant March, and it changed the overpayment by four hundred quid.
fieldNote: He's an **everyday AI user** who still builds checks around it.
He knows his weak spot is **the law** and plans to fix it.
Plenty of local jobs mean **boredom**, not fear, is his risk here.

steps.text: Take the department's debt recovery law course this winter
Keep putting a few hundred a month into index funds
Add a date-check step to the overpayments spreadsheet

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the one I think is happening. Overpayments is all checking and writing letters, so it's right in the firing line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to change how we work and we should get ahead of it, not fight it. At work I'd push to be on whatever pilot comes. Online I'd be realistic: some jobs shrink, and people need help moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm one of the safer juniors, because I'm the one who'll be setting the tools up. The people who won't touch them are in trouble. Fewer juniors get hired though, so it's not like the ladder stays the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my manager to put me on the automation project as soon as it starts. I'd do a short course on data and process design in the first six months. And I'd keep my investments as they are and keep six months of rent in cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I'd say. My own job looks okay, but the team around me shrinks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Karen, my senior. She's sharp on the law but she hates the tools. If they cut senior posts, she's exposed, and she's taught me most of what I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does it feel awkward being the one who builds the tool that shrinks the team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. I'd want to be honest with her. I'd offer to show my senior Karen the tools in exchange for the law, which is a fair trade.

say: We should **get ahead** of it, not fight it.
Some jobs shrink, and people **need help moving** into new work.
think: I'm one of the **safer juniors** because I'll set the tools up.
Fewer juniors hired means the **ladder changes** anyway.
do: Ask to join the **automation project** from day one.
Do a **process design** course in six months.
S1.quote: I'd offer to show my senior Karen the tools in exchange for the law, which is a fair trade.
fieldNote: He sees himself as **builder, not victim**, of the change.
He feels **some guilt** towards his senior and plans a fair swap.
His centre view: **get ahead**, help people move.

steps.text: Ask to join the overpayments automation project from day one
Do a short data and process design course in six months
Keep six months of rent in cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's a jolt, even for me. If it really can do any thinking work, it can do mine, including the bit I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a big deal and governments need to move fast on support, because most people won't be ready. Online I'd try not to sound smug about having used the tools early. Using early doesn't protect anyone if the end point is the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd have a year or two of work setting it up, then the overpayments team is basically gone. I'm not panicking, because I've got savings and no kids. But I'd lose my career path, and I'd need a new one fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say yes to every implementation role going, even temporary. I'd use some of my savings for a course in something where people want a human, maybe mediation, sorting out debt disputes face to face. And I'd move some shares out of the companies that will lose from this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd have some control, but it's a real drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any income you'd have that isn't from your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the money from the friend's app, if it worked. But honestly, a budgeting app is thinking work too. I wouldn't count on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've been ahead of others with AI. Does that stop mattering?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In a sense, yes. The quick-with-tools edge lasts about as long as the tools need people. That's the honest truth.

say: Governments need to **move fast** on support.
Using tools early **doesn't protect** anyone at the same end point.
think: I'd get **a year or two** of setup work, then the team goes.
I'm not panicking, but I'd **lose my career path**.
do: Pay for a **mediation course** from savings.
**Move some shares** out of firms that lose.
S2.quote: The quick-with-tools edge lasts about as long as the tools need people.
fieldNote: He's honest that **early adoption** buys only time.
He looks to **face-to-face mediation** as a human niche.
**No kids and savings** keep him from alarm.

steps.text: Take every AI implementation role on offer, even temporary
Pay for a mediation course from savings
Move some shares out of firms likely to lose

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is a much better runway. I'd be thirty-two when it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to do this properly: train people, plan services, look after claimants. At work I'd be pushing for a retraining fund. Online I'd be the boring one sharing actual plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd have three or four good years leading tool rollouts, and I'd learn a lot. Then I'd need to have moved somewhere human. I'm fairly confident I can do that in five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd lead the overpayments automation, get my name on it. By year two I'd start the mediation qualification part-time. I'd also try a small side business helping people sort out their own overpayment disputes, in the evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Things are moving around me, but I can see my next step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a side business in overpayment disputes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a real need. People get letters saying they owe two thousand pounds and they panic. Sitting with them and going through it is something I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Couldn't AI do that too, by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but people will want a person with them when the debt letter comes. I'd bet on that for a while.

say: We've got time to **do this properly**: train people and plan services.
I'd push for a **retraining fund** at work.
think: I'd get **three or four** good years leading rollouts.
I'm fairly confident I can **move somewhere human** in time.
do: **Lead the automation** in the first year.
Start a **mediation qualification** in year two.
Run an **evening side business** helping with disputes.
feel: **Uneasy**, but I can see **my next step**.
S3.quote: People get letters saying they owe two thousand pounds and they panic.
fieldNote: Five years lets him **build a reputation** before switching.
His side business idea comes from **real claimant panic**.
He bets on people wanting **a human** beside them.

steps.text: Lead the overpayments automation project in year one
Start a part-time mediation qualification in year two
Help people with overpayment disputes as an evening side business

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a career and a half at my age. I'd be thirty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version we can handle, so let's not waste it. I'd want the department to start planning now. Online I'd be quietly positive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I come out fine. Ten years to learn, lead and then shift. I'll lose this job eventually, but I'd have three moves planned by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI daily, get better on the law, and aim for senior caseworker in three years. Then I'd go into designing or auditing these systems. Savings stay invested.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. It actually looks good for someone like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I'd buy a flat instead of renting. Ten years of steady work is enough to get a mortgage sorted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You haven't mentioned robots. Do they matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's fair. The robots don't change my job much, because my job isn't hands-on. It's the thinking AI that matters for me, and that's 2036.

say: This is the **version we can handle**, so let's not waste it.
The department should **start planning** now, not in five years.
think: I come out **fine**: learn, lead, then shift.
I'd have **three moves** planned by the time this job ends.
do: Aim for **senior caseworker** within three years.
Move into **auditing AI systems** after that.
S4.quote: The robots don't change my job much, because my job isn't hands-on.
fieldNote: He's **genuinely calm** here, and it fits his savings and skills.
His concern is **thinking AI**, not robots.
He'd use the time to **climb then shift**.

steps.text: Aim for senior caseworker on overpayments within three years
Move into auditing benefit AI systems after that
Buy a flat instead of renting by the river

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one. Not because I'd be broke, but because I'd lose the path I'm on before I'd built the next one. What would help is a government retraining fund for public sector staff and a clear timetable for automation in each department.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about claimants who get overpaid because of a system error. If the machines make mistakes, someone has to own them. I'd want to know who that is before we switch anything on.

headlineQuote: If the machines make mistakes, someone has to own them.
portrait: A **27-year-old overpayments caseworker**, weak on the law but strong with tools.
He uses AI **every day** and built the team's repayment spreadsheet.
Savings, shares and **no kids** keep him calm or uneasy in most scenarios.
He sees himself as **leading rollouts**, then moving to human work like mediation.
Only fast AGI makes him **anxious**, because his career path vanishes.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his career path goes before he's built the next one.
whatWouldHelp: A **retraining fund** for public sector staff.
A **clear timetable** for automation in each department.
